verdicts.reason: Editorial, honestly labelled, and the explanation does the work the answer option does not. Options 2 and 3 overlap enough that a test-wise reader can pair-eliminate them, but option 1 is a genuine competitor.

The question says 'headphones', the answer says 'the rhythm you hear' — a podcast or audiobook has no rhythm, so the stem does not support the answer. Say 'music with a steady beat' in the question. Also soften the firmness: spontaneous (uninstructed) entrainment is modest and mainly occurs when the track's tempo is already close to your natural cadence, not for any tempo you play.
Mechanism and the ten-minute figure are both well supported, and the framing avoids any diet or medical advice. Distractor 0 is a bit of a throwaway but the other two are fair.

'What is the MOST COMMON reason people skip an outdoor walk' is an empirical claim about population frequency, answered from editorial opinion with no data behind it — exactly the over-firm framing the rubric warns about. Either cite survey evidence, or rewrite the stem as a claim you can actually stand behind, e.g. 'What is a common trap when deciding whether to walk outdoors?'

Source is Lally et al. 2010 (EJSP, doi 10.1002/ejsp.674) and it says what the item says: median 66 days, range 18-254. '21 days' is a genuinely attractive distractor, so the item is not a freebie despite being the only hedged option. Minor: explanation says 'studies' plural for one cited study.
Honestly labelled editorial, all four options are things people actually believe, and the explanation adds a reason rather than restating.

Half of this is evidence-backed and half is folklore presented as fact. Lally 2010 found a single missed opportunity did not materially affect habit formation — that part is fine. But 'two in a row is where a habit starts becoming a thing you used to do' is the 'never miss twice' rule of thumb from Atomic Habits / Tiny Habits, not a measured threshold, and it is baked into the correct option itself ('unless a second one follows'). Either drop the two-day threshold from the option and explanation, or mark it plainly as a rule of thumb rather than a finding.

Self-monitoring reactivity is well replicated, and the item is careful to say 'shift' rather than claiming a direction. No body or weight framing. Distractor 0 is true-but-not-an-answer, which is a good distractor rather than a bad one.

Source resolves to Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006, Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 38:69-119, d = .65 across 94 independent tests. 'Markedly increases' is a fair reading of a medium-to-large effect, not an overstatement.
Context-dependence of habit is solid, the simplification does not mislead, and the explanation names the mechanism (time, place, preceding event) instead of restating the option.
Editorial and correctly labelled. Safe, non-punitive, and 'do double to make up' is a real belief so the distractor earns its place.
Reasonable as simplified; option 2 is partly defensible but option 3 is clearly the better answer to the question as asked.

The question cannot be got wrong. 'How many days you turned up' is the definition of a streak, and the other three options are ruled out by simply knowing what the word means — no knowledge is tested. The point being made (a streak is not a fitness measure) is worth making, but make it the thing the reader has to work out: e.g. ask what a long streak does NOT tell you, or contrast two users with the same streak and different training.
Option 3 (people misjudge duration) is a real rival explanation rather than filler, which makes this a genuine question. Simplification is honest.

The claim is stated more firmly than the evidence supports, and probably backwards. Measured overnight muscle protein synthesis rates are LOW — lower than daytime and lower than post-absorptive morning values unless protein is given before sleep (Res et al. 2012; Trommelen & van Loon). Post-exercise synthesis is elevated across 24-48h, not concentrated in the hours you are asleep. 'Largely while you are asleep' is a gym truism, not a finding. What IS supportable: sleep restriction impairs training adaptation and growth-hormone pulses occur in slow-wave sleep. Rewrite around 'recovery depends on sleep' rather than 'most repair happens during sleep', or reject the item.

Standard adaptation framing, true at the level given. Option 0 is also true but less fundamental, which is the right shape for a distractor. Explanation adds the signal/response idea rather than restating.

Two problems. (1) Guessable: three of the four options are absolutes ('reliably', 'for anybody', 'always'), so the hedged one is identifiable as correct without knowing anything about sleep. Rewrite the distractors as specific, non-absolute claims. (2) The confidence label is wrong. `contested` requires the text to say the field disagrees; this explanation describes individual variation instead. And the field is not especially divided — Stutz et al. 2019 (Sports Med) found evening exercise does not generally harm sleep, with impairment mainly after vigorous exercise ending under an hour before bed. Relabel as `simplified` and consider naming that one-hour window, which is the actually useful fact here.
Definition is accurate, all four options are things the term could plausibly mean, and the explanation gives a usable test ('not enough to need recovering from').

Correctly kills the lactic-acid myth, which is worth the reader's attention. 'Follows the repair, not the effort' is a fair simplification of the damage-and-inflammation account, and option 3 is a genuinely tempting distractor.
True, useful, and safely framed — it defuses the 'no pain no gain' belief without shaming anyone. The two 'Yes' options are beliefs people really hold.

Source is Van Dongen et al. 2003, Sleep 26(2):117-26, and it does support the specific claim that subjective alertness ratings fail to track the objective deficit. The 0-vs-3 distinction is a real one, so the item tests something.
Sensible as simplified, no sleep-hygiene overclaiming, and the explanation gives the reason (you can decide to get up, not to fall asleep) rather than restating the option.
